title: State Management — Redux, Zustand, React Query

topics.title: What is Redux and how does React use it?
topics.html:
Redux is a predictable state container. All shared state lives in one object, and the only way to change it is to send a plain action object through a reducer.

  • Store — one object that holds the whole state of the app ("single source of truth").
  • Action — a plain object that describes what happened: { type: "cart/added", payload: item }. It says what happened, not how to change the state.
  • Reducer — a pure function (state, action) => newState. No API calls, no random values, no mutation — same input always gives the same output.
  • Dispatch — the only way in. You cannot write to the store directly.
  • Data flow is one direction: UI → dispatch(action) → reducer → new state → React re-renders. This is why you can log every change, replay it, and use time-travel debugging.

How React connects to it (react-redux):

  • <Provider store={store}> puts the store into context once, at the root.
  • useSelector reads a piece of state and subscribes the component to it. The component re-renders only when that piece changes, compared with ===.
  • useDispatch gives you the dispatch function to send actions.
  • Internally react-redux subscribes through useSyncExternalStore, because the store lives outside React.
// store
const store = configureStore({ reducer: { cart: cartReducer } });

// root
<Provider store={store}><App /></Provider>

// component
function CartBadge() {
  const count = useSelector((s: RootState) => s.cart.items.length); // subscribe
  const dispatch = useDispatch();
  return <button onClick={() => dispatch(cleared())}>{count}</button>;   // change
}

// select a small value, not the whole object
const items = useSelector(s => s.cart.items);            // ok — reference is stable
const bad = useSelector(s => s.cart.items.filter(i => i.active)); // new array every time → re-render always
💬 Say it like this

Redux keeps all shared state in one store, and the only way to change it is to dispatch an action — a plain object that describes what happened. A reducer takes the current state and that action and returns a new state. It is a pure function, so the same input always gives the same result.

React connects to it through react-redux. The Provider puts the store in context, useSelector reads one piece of state and subscribes the component to it, and useDispatch sends actions. The data flow is always one direction: the UI dispatches, the reducer returns new state, React re-renders.

The main benefit is predictability — every change is a logged event, so you can see exactly what happened and even replay it. The main cost is boilerplate, which is why nobody writes plain Redux any more; we use Redux Toolkit.

Why must a reducer be pure and immutable?
Purity makes state changes replayable and testable, and it is what makes DevTools time travel possible. Immutability is how React and useSelector detect a change — they compare references with ===, so changing an object in place is invisible.
Where do API calls go then?
Not in reducers. Side effects live in middleware — thunks, RTK Query, or Saga on older projects. The reducer only reacts to the actions those produce.
Do you still need Redux in 2026?
Much less often. React Query covers server state and Zustand covers simple client state. Redux still fits large apps with complex client state, many teams and a need for strict conventions and time-travel debugging.

topics.title: Why is Redux efficient at managing state, and how does that connect to React Fiber?
topics.html:
Redux itself is only a store plus a list of subscribers. The efficiency comes from where the subscription happens: every component subscribes on its own, so a dispatch wakes up only the components that really use the changed data.

dispatch(action) ↓ reducer returns a NEW state object (immutability — new reference) ↓ store notifies its subscribers ↓ each useSelector runs its selector and compares the result with === ↓ changed? no → component does nothing at all yes → setState → React schedules work on THAT component's fiber ↓ React renders that fiber and its children, diffs, commits to the DOM
  • Compared with Context: a new context value re-renders every consumer in the subtree. Redux does not use context for the data — the Provider only passes the store object once, and each useSelector keeps its own subscription. So one dispatch can re-render three components out of five hundred.
  • The link to Fiber is the update, not the store. When a selector result changes, react-redux calls a state update, and React turns it into a unit of work on that component's fiber node, with a priority (lane). React then builds a work-in-progress tree starting from that fiber, and commits the difference to the DOM.
  • Bail-out is the other half. While rendering, if a child's props and state have not changed by reference, React can reuse the existing fiber and skip that subtree. That is exactly why Redux insists on immutability: a mutated object keeps the same reference, so both useSelector and the fiber bail-out conclude that nothing changed, and the screen shows stale data.
  • Batching: since React 18 several dispatches in the same event — or in a promise, a timeout, a native handler — are batched into a single render pass, so five actions cost one render instead of five.
  • Concurrent rendering and tearing: Fiber can pause in the middle of a render. If an external store changed during that pause, one component could render old data and its sibling new data in the same frame. That is why react-redux reads the store through useSyncExternalStore — it guarantees one consistent snapshot for the whole render, and forces a synchronous re-render if the store moved.
  • Notification order: react-redux notifies parents before children. Otherwise a child could re-render with data whose parent has already decided to unmount it — the "zombie child" problem.
// what makes it fast in practice
const total = useSelector(s => s.cart.total);      // one primitive → compared with ===
const items = useSelector(selectVisibleItems);      // createSelector → stable reference

// what makes it slow
const state = useSelector(s => s);                  // re-renders on every action
const visible = useSelector(s => s.cart.items.filter(i => i.active)); // new array every time

// mutation kills both useSelector and the fiber bail-out
state.items.push(item);        // ✗ same reference → React sees no change
state.items = [...state.items, item];  // ✓ new reference → update propagates
💬 Say it like this

Redux is efficient because the subscription is per component, not per tree. The Provider only passes the store down once. Each useSelector subscribes on its own, runs its selector after every action and compares the result by reference. If the result is the same, that component does nothing — no render at all. With plain Context every consumer re-renders when the value changes, so Redux scales much better for frequent updates.

The connection with Fiber is on the update side. When a selector result changes, react-redux triggers a state update, and React turns it into work on that component's fiber, with a priority. React then re-renders that fiber and its children and commits only the real DOM changes. While it renders, it can bail out of any subtree whose props did not change by reference — and this is exactly why reducers must be immutable. If I mutate the state, the reference stays the same, so both the selector check and the fiber bail-out think nothing happened, and the UI shows old data.

The last part is concurrent rendering. Fiber can pause a render in the middle, and the Redux store lives outside React, so it could change during that pause. That would show two different values in the same frame — this is called tearing. react-redux solves it with useSyncExternalStore, which gives React one consistent snapshot for the whole render.

So is Redux faster than Context?
For frequently changing shared state, usually yes — because it re-renders only the subscribed components instead of the whole consumer subtree. For rarely changing values like theme or locale, Context is simpler and the difference does not matter.
What is the most common Redux performance bug?
A selector that creates a new object or array on every call. The reference is always different, so === always fails and the component re-renders on every action. Fix it with createSelector or by selecting smaller values.
Does Redux work with concurrent features like useTransition?
Yes, but external store updates are not time-sliced — useSyncExternalStore has to keep the snapshot consistent, so those updates are processed with high priority instead of being spread across frames.

topics.title: Redux Toolkit vs Zustand vs React Query — how do you choose?
topics.html:
• Server state (API data): React Query. Cache, invalidation, background refetch, optimistic updates. Replaces 80% of what Redux did.
  • Client state (UI state): Zustand for local/modular, minimal boilerplate. Redux Toolkit for complex global state in large teams needing time-travel debugging.
  • Context API: fine for low-frequency globals (theme, locale, current user). Bad as general state.
// Zustand store
const useAuthStore = create<AuthState>()(devtools(persist(
  (set) => ({ user: null, token: null, login: (user, token) => set({ user, token }), logout: () => set({ user: null, token: null }) }),
  { name: "auth-storage" }
)));
// React Query optimistic update
const toggleLike = useMutation({
  mutationFn: (id: string) => api.toggleLike(id),
  onMutate: async (id) => {
    await queryClient.cancelQueries({ queryKey: ["posts"] });
    const prev = queryClient.getQueryData(["posts"]);
    queryClient.setQueryData(["posts"], (old: Post[]) => old.map(p => p.id === id ? { ...p, liked: !p.liked } : p));
    return { prev };
  },
  onError: (_e, _v, ctx) => queryClient.setQueryData(["posts"], ctx?.prev),
  onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ["posts"] }),
});
💬 Say it like this

I think about state in three buckets: server state, client state, and URL state. Server state is anything that lives in a database — it's async, it can go stale, it needs caching. React Query handles that perfectly. Client state is pure UI — is this modal open, what tab is selected. Zustand is my go-to: minimal boilerplate, works great with TypeScript. I reach for Redux Toolkit only when the team is large and needs time-travel debugging, or when there are very complex state interactions.

topics.title: Redux Toolkit — what is inside it and how do you use it well?
topics.html:
• createSlice gives you the reducer and the actions together. Inside a reducer you can write code that looks like mutation — Immer records it and produces a new state object, so the store stays immutable.
  • configureStore sets up DevTools, thunk and dev-only checks for non-serializable values. Keep only plain data in the store: no Dates, class instances, Promises or functions.
  • Async: createAsyncThunk for one-off side effects, RTK Query when the data comes from an API — it gives you caching, refetching and loading states, so you stop writing three actions per request.
  • Selectors: keep them next to the slice and memoize the ones that compute something (createSelector). A selector that returns a new object or array on every call will re-render the component every time.
  • Normalize lists with createEntityAdapter ({ ids, entities }) so updating one item does not touch the whole array.
  • When Redux is still the right answer: big team, complex client state, strict conventions, time-travel debugging, or a lot of logic that must be testable outside components.
const cartSlice = createSlice({
  name: "cart",
  initialState: { items: [] as Item[] },
  reducers: {
    added(state, action: PayloadAction<Item>) {
      state.items.push(action.payload);   // looks like mutation, Immer makes it immutable
    },
    removed(state, action: PayloadAction<string>) {
      state.items = state.items.filter(i => i.id !== action.payload);
    },
  },
});
export const { added, removed } = cartSlice.actions;
// memoized selector — recomputes only when items change
export const selectTotal = createSelector(
  (s: RootState) => s.cart.items,
  items => items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0)
);
💬 Say it like this

Redux Toolkit is the modern way to write Redux. createSlice gives me the reducer and the actions in one place, and Immer lets me write simple code like state.items.push() while the store stays immutable underneath.

Two things I am careful about. First, only plain data goes into the store. Second, selectors that calculate something must be memoized with createSelector, because a selector that returns a new array every time will re-render the component on every action.

For server data I do not write thunks any more. I use RTK Query or React Query, because caching and refetching are already solved there.

Why is mutation allowed in createSlice?
It is not real mutation. Immer gives the reducer a draft proxy, records the changes and returns a new state object. Outside a reducer the same code would be a bug.
RTK Query or React Query?
RTK Query if the project is already on Redux — one store, one DevTools. React Query if there is no Redux, or if the client state is small enough that Redux is not needed at all.

topics.title: Zustand — how does it work, and where do people get it wrong?
topics.html:
• The store is a hook. No provider, no context, no boilerplate. It lives outside React, so you can also read and update it from a plain function with useAuthStore.getState().
  • Always select what you need. const user = useStore(s => s.user) re-renders only when user changes. const store = useStore() re-renders on every change — this is the mistake people make first.
  • If a selector returns a new object, pass a shallow comparator (useShallow), otherwise the reference is different every render and the component never stops re-rendering.
  • Middleware: persist for localStorage, devtools for Redux DevTools, immer if you prefer draft-style updates.
  • Big stores are split with the slices pattern: several small creator functions combined into one store.
  • Trade-off vs Redux: much less code and no conventions enforced — which is great in a small team and risky in a large one, because nothing stops people from putting anything anywhere.
const useCartStore = create<CartState>()(devtools(persist((set, get) => ({
  items: [],
  add: (item) => set({ items: [...get().items, item] }),
  clear: () => set({ items: [] }),
}), { name: "cart" })));
// GOOD — subscribes to one field
const count = useCartStore(s => s.items.length);
// BAD — re-renders on any change in the store
const { items } = useCartStore();
// object selector needs a shallow compare
const { add, clear } = useCartStore(useShallow(s => ({ add: s.add, clear: s.clear })));
💬 Say it like this

Zustand is a small store that you use as a hook. There is no provider and almost no boilerplate, and the store also works outside React, which is handy in event handlers or in an API layer.

The important rule is to always subscribe with a selector. If I call the store without one, the component re-renders on every change anywhere in the store. And if my selector returns a new object, I use a shallow comparison, otherwise the reference changes every render.

I pick Zustand when the client state is simple and the team is small, and Redux Toolkit when we need strict structure and shared conventions across many people.

How do you test components that use a Zustand store?
Reset the store between tests with setState and the initial state, or create the store per test and inject it. Because the store is a module singleton, state leaks between tests if you forget.
Do you still need React Query with Zustand?
Yes. Zustand holds client state; it has no cache, no refetching and no request deduplication. Server data still belongs in React Query.
